extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy/history/sociology of science; readers interested in evolutionary models of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for judging or constructing accounts that use evolutionary theory to explain scientific change, progress, and the dynamics of scientific communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad appeal to evolutionary ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate evolutionary account of science should 'appeal to as broad of a range of evolutionary ideas as I can' rather than restrict itself narrowly to a small subset of evolutionary concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit the analogy to a single mechanism (e.g., selection). Consider multiple evolutionary concepts (selection, inheritance mechanisms, drift, divergence, carrying capacity, etc.) to allow the analogy to suggest novel pathways for inquiry and explanation. Balance reader patience with conceptual breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection as a component, not the whole story
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection should have a 'prominent place' but not be treated as the only or overwhelmingly dominant process in accounts of scientific change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model selection as appearing in greater or lesser degrees depending on context; explicitly recognize contexts where selection is relatively insignificant and account for non-selective mechanisms that shape scientific knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of phenomena analyzed
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework should be applied to a wide range of scientific practices and historical patterns rather than to a narrow set of epistemic phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use documented trends from history and sociology of science as data; test the analogy across many domains to show its generative potential rather than restricting it to exceptional case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical payoff (must solve or illuminate problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: The evolutionary analogy must do philosophical work: it should explain things about science we did not previously understand and shed light on broader philosophical problems, not merely redescribe familiar phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the account offers genuine explanatory advantage (new answers, new distinctions) over non-evolutionary accounts. An analogy that offers no novel explanations is philosophically weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real directionality from pseudodirectionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts must be able to distinguish genuine directional change (real directionality) from 'pseudodirectionality' produced by historiographical selection and retrospective narrative smoothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to historical narrativization: textbooks and histories often manufacture linear progress by emphasizing antecedents that fit current consensus and suppressing messy or irrelevant antecedents. Demonstrate causal processes that genuinely produce increases in epistemic well‑foundedness rather than post-hoc story-telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain vertical and horizontal directionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish and account for two types of directionality: (1) vertical — increasing degrees of refinement or specialization; (2) horizontal — increasing kinds or branches of specialization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful explanation should show how evolutionary mechanisms generate both increases in depth (refinement) and breadth (branching) of scientific knowledge, and when each type is expected to occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for sociocultural (nonepistemic) directionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some directional patterns in science may be driven by sociocultural pressures that are not themselves epistemic and may vary orthogonally to epistemic improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether changes in scientific direction are responses to broader cultural or institutional currents (e.g., Forman's claim about early quantum theory in post-WWI Germany). Show how sociocultural pressures can produce directionality that does not correspond to epistemic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and identify epistemic pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: A pressure is epistemic iff adaptation to it is explained by increases in the depth or breadth of our knowledge; increases in depth or breadth count as improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this operational definition to identify which pressures driving scientific change are genuinely epistemic (i.e., their causal role is to produce better or broader knowledge) versus those that are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vs external pressures (internality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pressure is internal to science iff adaptation to it is explained by achievements that are recognizably important to most practitioners but not to most nonpractitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the pressures counted as internal are tied to practitioners' epistemic aims (e.g., technical results valued within the field). Distinguish these from external/sociocultural pressures that explain direction without reference to practitioners' epistemic priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account must accommodate nonadaptive features
rubrics_metrics.description: An evolutionary account must not ignore nonadaptive features of scientific practice; nonadaptive phenomena are part of the growth process and must be included as legitimate targets of explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how nonadaptive patterns (those not explained by adaptation) arise and how they fit into the broader evolutionary picture of science's development rather than treating them as anomalies to be discarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative case selection (avoid unrepresentative cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case studies used to motivate the analogy should be representative of scientific practice; atypical or extreme historical episodes (e.g., the systematics/cladistics wars) can mislead about general dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer cases that reflect ordinary scientific social dynamics; when using highly conflictual or unusual cases, explicitly justify their relevance and limitations for general theory-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on the replicator/interactor framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely exclusively on the replicator/interactor vocabulary if it obscures connections to the broader conceptual foundations of evolutionary theory or makes the analogy less recognizable to evolutionary theorists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using replicator terminology, acknowledge its limits (it mainly represents selection) and consider alternative framings that better map onto classical evolutionary theory so experts in evolution can readily recognize the analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate that scientific knowledge satisfies Darwinian population conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain directionality as an evolutionary result, show that scientific knowledge (or practices) can be treated as a Darwinian population—i.e., that it meets general constraints enabling evolution by natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide independent evidence that scientific practices/knowledge exhibit the causal connectedness, variation, differential 'reproductive' success, and inheritance required for selection-like processes to operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heredity (H)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heredity: the extent to which offspring resemble parents due to the causal role of parents (one of Godfrey‑Smith's components for Darwinian populations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show mechanisms by which elements of scientific practice or content are transmitted (e.g., training, publications, norms, citations) so that instances resemble antecedent instances in properties relevant to 'fitness' (propensity to produce more instances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsicality (S)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsicality (S): the extent to which differences in reproductive output depend on intrinsic features of the members of the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that intrinsic properties of scientific practices/ideas (not merely external accidents) causally influence their propensity to 'reproduce' (be adopted, copied, extended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity (C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity (C): the extent to which the magnitude of trait differences tracks the magnitude of their fitness differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidence that small differences among practice-instances or ideas correspond to proportionate differences in their success (adoption, persistence), supporting gradual adaptive change rather than purely discontinuous shifts.
